column3: It presents reminder as a means of cultivating God-consciousness, contrasting those screened from God's reminder.
It immediately precedes the focus in the final judgment sequence that gathers the disbelievers later identified here.
Turning away from obedience supplies a general behavioral counterpart to the focus's settled refusal of divine remembrance.
The inability of idols to give help does not clarify human blindness or deafness toward remembrance.
Its temporary divinely imposed sealing of the sleepers' ears is the explicit narrative contrast to the focus's enduring inability to hear.
It defines the revealed Reminder as something explained so people may reflect, the receptivity lacking in the focus.
The idols' inability to help concerns neither remembrance nor human sensory-spiritual closure.
It introduces Hell for the disbelievers whom the next ayah characterizes by their veiled sight and failed hearing.
The command to obey God and the Messenger gives the positive response opposed to turning from His reminder.
The devils' inability to bring revelation is unrelated to the focus's inability to hear it.
It closely parallels the focus: turning from God's signs results in coverings over hearts and heaviness in ears against understanding.
The opening of the Dhul-Qarnayn account calls it a reminder, preparing the phrase "My reminder" at the account's close.
It directly pairs turning from "My reminder" with a punitive blindness at resurrection.
The immediate continuation identifies the same disbelievers by their false loyalties and confirms their prepared punishment.
The removal of a covering that makes sight sharp at judgment is a close reversal of eyes covered from remembrance.
It describes condemned people as unable to hear and unable to see, closely matching the focus's sensory-spiritual incapacity.
It immediately develops the identity and loss of the disbelievers introduced in the focus.
Its command to remind establishes the constructive purpose of remembrance that the focus's people cannot receive.
It warns against claiming to hear while not truly hearing, directly clarifying the focus's failed hearing.
It immediately describes the worldly loss and self-deception of the group in the focus.
It contrasts turning away with obedience that leads to guidance, framing the response absent from the focus.
The image of obliterated eyes and consequent inability to see offers a physical analogy for the focus's veiled sight.
It immediately names disbelief in God's signs and meeting as the cause of the group's worthless deeds.
It explicitly concerns one who turns away from God's remembrance and confines desire to worldly life.
It explains how granted hearing, sight, and hearts fail when people deny God's signs, closely paralleling the focus.
It immediately states Hell as the recompense for mocking God's signs and messengers.
It presents guidance and reminder as effective for people of understanding, contrasting the focus's closed perception.
Its altered visual perception in battle is not a close explanation of being veiled from remembrance.
It supplies the faithful and righteous counterpart to the disbelievers described in the focus.
Misplaced obedience can return believers to disbelief, a broad parallel to abandoning right guidance.
The punitive wiping of eyes is a limited physical parallel to the focus's covered eyes.
The permanence of the believers' reward continues the contrast with the focused disbelievers' coming punishment.
A people misled into obeying Pharaoh illustrate misdirected allegiance, only indirectly related to the focus.
Material inability to travel does not clarify spiritual inability to hear.
The inexhaustibility of God's words broadly reinforces the value of the divine message, without addressing rejection.
Obeying disbelievers leading to loss is only a general contrast in chosen direction.
It calls prior warnings a reminder and affirms divine justice, relevant to the focus's judgment context.
The surah's closing call to worship God sincerely gives the positive response to the focus's rejection.
The trusted angel's being obeyed does not clarify human reception of remembrance.
Faith and God-consciousness alone do not specifically illuminate the focus's sensory-spiritual closure.
The parable of fleeting worldly life may underlie distraction from remembrance but has no direct sensory link.
The repeated command to obey offers only a broad positive counterpart to refusal.
The wish for death is unrelated to the focus.
The rejection of a chosen bearer of the reminder illustrates a social form of resisting its message.
Rescue of believing, God-conscious people adds no specific link to remembrance or perception.
Collective obedience is a broad positive counterpart, without clarifying the focus's blindness and deafness.
It explicitly warns against one whose heart is made heedless of God's remembrance and who follows desire.
The command to obey a messenger is only a general positive counterpart.
Rescue of believers does not specifically clarify the focus.
Unaccepted hypocritical spending only broadly concerns an inwardly deficient response.
The description of believing submitters has no specific connection to remembrance or perception.
The command to obey is a broad positive counterpart to turning away.
It identifies attentive listening and a present heart as the conditions in which reminder benefits, directly reversing the focus.
The command to obey is a broad positive counterpart to turning away.
Eyes responding with tears on hearing recognized truth provide a vivid positive contrast to covered eyes and failed hearing.
Its call to remember from first creation is relevant only through the general vocabulary of remembrance.
The Sabbath test narrative does not clarify blindness or deafness toward God's reminder.
The command to obey is a broad positive counterpart to turning away.
Eyes rolling in fear describe panic, not perceptual closure toward divine remembrance.
The Quran being made easy for remembrance contrasts the accessible message with those unable to receive it.
Hell as a place lying in wait supports the immediate judgment setting but adds little to the focus's cause.
The command to obey is a broad positive counterpart to turning away.
It depicts arrogant people turned from God's signs, rejecting guidance and remaining heedless, closely matching the focus.
It describes reminder becoming beneficial when a person actually remembers, the response blocked in the focus.
It presents the prophetic message as a reminder for all peoples, contrasting the focus's refusal of God's reminder.
It defines revelation as a reminder for the receptive and God-fearing, opposed to the focus's closed condition.
It calls the warning a reminder for humanity but does not closely address the focus's refusal.
The command to obey is a broad positive counterpart to turning away.
Following the revealed light through the Messenger provides a positive counterpart to being veiled from God's reminder.
It presents revelation as warning and reminder, with reception varying by the hearer's disposition.
Inability to prostrate on the Day of Judgment does not explain inability to hear remembrance.
The command to obey is a broad positive counterpart to turning away.
Inability to repel sudden punishment does not clarify the focus's perceptual state.
It explicitly links repeated trials, failure to repent, and failure to remember.
Covenant-breaking does not specifically clarify the focus's blindness or deafness.
Moses's lack of patience in a teaching episode is unrelated to the focus's inability to hear.
It contrasts physical looking with not seeing and calls such people blind to guidance, closely paralleling the focus.
Clear verses given so people may remember offer only a general positive relation.
It locates disbelievers in heedlessness before the Day of Regret, supporting the focus's judgment context.
It contrasts turning away with the Messenger's clear delivery, which the focus's people fail to receive.
It links apostasy with hearts being sealed and consequent failure to understand, closely matching the focus's closure.
Inability to retrieve vanished water is unrelated to hearing or remembrance.
It explicitly says they neither hear guidance nor truly see despite appearing to look.
The barrier's resistance to climbing or piercing has no meaningful relation to the focus.
Inability to make a bequest at sudden death is unrelated to the focus.
It identifies the revelation as a reminder for all worlds, a general counterpoint to those cut off from it.
It joins sealed hearts, hearing, and sight with heedlessness, making it a close conceptual parallel.
The reward of obeying God and the Messenger is a broad positive counterpart.
Inability to speak after judgment does not clarify the focus's prior inability to hear.
God's preservation of the Reminder contrasts its enduring availability with the focus's refusal to access it.
The plotters' lack of awareness is not a useful relation to the focus.
Rejecting disbelievers' direction is only a broad contrast in allegiance.
Reciting God's book and practicing devotion are a general positive counterpart without a close link.
The recited Book functions as mercy and reminder for believers, contrasting the focus's blocked reception.
Later disagreement after knowledge does not specifically clarify the focus.
It calls the revealed accounts a divinely given reminder, directly relating the surrounding Dhul-Qarnayn narrative to remembrance.
Lack of fear for the Hereafter may underlie rejection, but it is not a close explanation here.
Its command to listen and obey describes the active response opposite to the focus's inability to hear.
The pleasant life of the righteous does not clarify the focus.
Satan causing people to forget God's remembrance directly explains a pathway into the focus's estrangement from it.
God's sealing of hearts and hearing, with a covering over sight, is a direct conceptual parallel to the focus's closed eyes and hearing.
The description of people as deaf, dumb, and blind vividly characterizes entrenched refusal of guidance.
It compares disbelievers to those who hear only a call and cry, yet are deaf, dumb, and blind to its meaning.
It links rejection and disbelief with hearts being covered, closely paralleling the focus's inability to receive remembrance.
It records people becoming blind and deaf after assuming they would not be tested, a close sensory-spiritual parallel.
It explicitly places coverings over hearts against understanding and deafness in ears when Quranic signs are recited.
It distinguishes those who truly listen and respond from those who remain unresponsive until judgment.
It describes those who deny the signs as deaf, dumb, and in darkness, directly supporting the focus's condition.
It contrasts seeing the divine insights with remaining blind, a useful counterpart to eyes veiled from remembrance.
It describes hearts and eyes being turned away because of initial disbelief, then being left wandering blindly.
It explicitly describes people with hearts that do not understand, eyes that do not see, and ears that do not hear.
It asks whether the deaf can be made to hear even when they do not understand, directly clarifying failed hearing of guidance.
Its contrast between the blind and deaf and those who see and hear presents the two opposed responses to revelation.
The contrast between blind and seeing people, and between darkness and light, provides a compact analogy for the focus.
It contrasts one who knows the revealed truth with one who is blind, connecting sight to recognition of revelation.
It places a hidden veil between Quranic recitation and those who disbelieve in the Hereafter, closely matching the focus's covering.
It describes coverings on hearts against understanding and heaviness in ears when God alone is mentioned.
It makes worldly blindness the basis for greater blindness and loss in the Hereafter, extending the focus's present condition.
It describes the misguided as resurrected blind, dumb, and deaf, linking rejected guidance with final judgment.
The question of being raised blind despite formerly seeing directly develops the consequence of turning from remembrance.
It answers that divine signs were forgotten, so the person is forgotten, completing the same warning as the focus.
It calls for travel so hearts may understand and ears may hear, explicitly locating blindness in hearts rather than physical eyes.
The granting of hearing, sight, and hearts establishes these faculties as capacities for grateful, responsive reception.
It states that many neither hear nor understand, reducing them to a more astray condition and closely echoing failed reception.
It says the dead and the deaf cannot be made to hear when they turn away, closely paralleling the focus's inability to hear.
It repeats that neither the dead nor deaf fleeing away can be made to hear the call, reinforcing the same condition.
The gift of hearing, sight, and hearts contrasts divine provision of receptive faculties with the focus's misuse of them.
It condemns one reminded of God's signs who then turns away, directly supplying the volitional root of the focus's closure.
The blind and seeing are set in contrast, giving a concise perceptual image for spiritual discernment.
A covering placed before and behind people causes them not to see, a limited but vivid analogy for the focus's veiled eyes.
It contrasts one opened to Islam with those whose hearts are hardened against God's remembrance.
It depicts people recoiling when God alone is mentioned, a behavioral expression of estrangement from remembrance.
It combines covered hearts, deaf ears, and a veil between hearers and messenger, making it a very close parallel.
It describes a Quranic message as deafness in some ears and blindness to its recipients, directly matching the focus.
It joins following desire with a seal on hearing and heart and a covering over sight, closely explaining the focus's state.
It describes those rejected by God as made deaf and blinded in their vision.
The question whether people will reflect on the Quran or have locks on hearts targets the inward barrier behind failed reception.
The Quran's being made easy for remembrance contrasts its accessibility with the focus's refusal to receive it.
It warns believers not to let hearts harden so they become unlike earlier people who forgot the reminder.
Forgetting God causes people to forget themselves, a direct companion formulation to being cut off from God's remembrance.
The condemned admit that listening or reasoning would have prevented their fate, directly opposing the focus's inability to hear.
It depicts a people who block their ears, cover themselves, persist, and grow arrogant when called to forgiveness.
It portrays people turning away from the reminder, providing a concise behavioral parallel to the focus.
It explicitly identifies the revelation as a reminder, clarifying the object from which the focus's people are screened.
